_doc: Verified published works grounding the menu-pricing study. Economics + food science. Every citation adversarially verified (existence + attribution + finding); each renders with its DOI/identifier for reader verification.

studies.authors: N. Gregory Mankiw
studies.title: Small Menu Costs and Large Business Cycles: A Macroeconomic Model of Monopoly
studies.venue: The Quarterly Journal of Economics, vol. 100, no. 2, pp. 529-538 (MIT Press at time of publication; QJE now published by Oxford University Press)
studies.finding: In a monopoly model, a small fixed cost of changing the posted price makes it privately rational for a firm to leave its price unchanged after a nominal demand shock, yet the resulting price rigidity produces welfare losses far larger than the menu cost itself.
studies.groundsHow: Our print-vs-float posture rests directly on Mankiw's result that a small fixed repricing cost rationally justifies holding a listed price through a shock; we carry it from macro monopoly theory into the concrete menu-reprint decision.
studies.myth: The popular reading that a 'menu cost' is merely the trivial expense of reprinting menus — Mankiw's point is the opposite: even small repricing frictions (a metaphor for all adjustment costs) generate disproportionately large effects, so the cost is neither trivial nor merely physical.

studies.authors: Mark Bils and Peter J. Klenow
studies.title: Some Evidence on the Importance of Sticky Prices
studies.venue: Journal of Political Economy, vol. 112, no. 5, pp. 947-985 (University of Chicago Press)
studies.finding: Using BLS micro-data on ~350 categories (about 70% of consumer spending), the median price spell lasts about 4.3 months including temporary sales and about 5.5 months once sales are excluded, with the frequency of price change differing dramatically across goods.
studies.groundsHow: Gives our 'don't reprint on day one' posture an empirical cadence: even in a broad, relatively flexible sample, half of prices persist 4-5+ months — long enough that a short cost shock usually resolves before a disciplined operator would otherwise reprice.

studies.authors: Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson
studies.title: Five Facts about Prices: A Reevaluation of Menu Cost Models
studies.venue: The Quarterly Journal of Economics, vol. 123, no. 4, pp. 1415-1464 (MIT Press at time of publication; QJE now published by Oxford University Press)
studies.finding: Re-examining the same class of BLS micro-data, once temporary sales are excluded the median frequency of regular (nonsale) price change is roughly half the with-sales frequency, implying regular prices persist on the order of 8-11 months, and the price-change hazard does not rise with time since the last change.
studies.groundsHow: Our strongest anchor for holding through a shock: stripping out promo sales shows regular list prices persist most of a year, so a 77-day median shock will typically pass before a reprint is warranted — the empirical spine of 'don't reprint on day one.'
studies.myth: The widely repeated claim that Bils-Klenow prove prices 'change every ~4 months, so prices are basically flexible' — Nakamura-Steinsson show most of that churn is temporary sales snapping back to a sticky regular price, so regular prices are roughly twice as sticky (median ~8-11 months).

studies.authors: Alan S. Blinder, Elie R. D. Canetti, David E. Lebow, and Jeremy B. Rudd
studies.title: Asking About Prices: A New Approach to Understanding Price Stickiness
studies.finding: In structured interviews with ~200 U.S. firms testing twelve theories of price stickiness, most firms reported repricing no more than once or twice a year (many only annually), and the best-supported explanations were coordination failure (waiting for rivals to move first) and implicit contracts / not antagonizing customers rather than the physical cost of changing prices.
studies.groundsHow: Validates our posture with operator testimony: experienced price-setters deliberately hold prices roughly annually and cite relational/strategic frictions, which is exactly why we counsel floating quietly rather than reprinting the menu at the first cost move.
studies.myth: That 'menu costs' are dominated by the physical cost of changing price tags or menus — Blinder's survey ranked such physical costs low; the binding frictions are informational and relational (coordination failure, customer goodwill).

studies.authors: Michael L. Kasavana; Donald I. Smith
studies.title: Menu Engineering: A Practical Guide to Menu Analysis
studies.venue: Hospitality Publications, Okemos, MI (book; framework developed at the Michigan State University School of Hospitality Business)
studies.id: OCLC 9550099 — https://search.worldcat.org/title/9550099 (ISBN 0-932235-01-5 / 9780932235015; also Open Library OL21382210M)
studies.finding: Introduced menu engineering: every item is plotted on two axes — menu mix (popularity) and contribution margin (gross profit dollars per item) — into Stars (popular, high-margin), Plowhorses (popular, low-margin), Puzzles (unpopular, high-margin), and Dogs (unpopular, low-margin), each carrying a distinct reprice/reposition/keep/cut action.
studies.groundsHow: Our per-item posture verdict (hold / reprice / reposition / cut) is the direct descendant of their popularity x contribution-margin quadrant; we extend it by driving the margin axis with live cost-index movement instead of a static food cost.
studies.myth: Corrects the older 'lowest food-cost-percentage item is the most profitable' rule: menu engineering ranks on contribution-margin dollars, not food-cost %, so a low-cost-% item can still be a weak contributor and a high-cost-% item a strong one.

studies.authors: Sybil S. Yang; Sheryl E. Kimes; Mauro M. Sessarego
studies.title: Menu price presentation influences on consumer purchase behavior in restaurants
studies.venue: International Journal of Hospitality Management, 28(1), 157-160 (peer-reviewed; companion Cornell Hospitality Report 9(8), '$ or Dollars: Effects of Menu-price Formats on Restaurant Checks')
studies.finding: In a field experiment at the Culinary Institute of America's teaching restaurant (~201 dining parties), guests handed menus with numeral-only prices (no '$', no 'dollars') spent modestly more (~8%) than guests whose menus carried a monetary cue; critically, the '$' symbol and the spelled-out word 'dollars' depressed checks about equally, implicating the monetary cue / 'pain of paying' rather than the glyph itself.
studies.groundsHow: Grounds the final rendering step of a printed price: once a posture fixes a price point, how the number is set (dropping the currency cue) is a lever — we cite it as a modest, context-bounded nudge, never a guaranteed lift.
studies.myth: Corrects the viral 'drop the dollar sign and diners spend more' law: it was a single upscale restaurant, the omnibus test of price presentation was not statistically significant, and the effect traces to any monetary cue (word or symbol), so it is small and not established as generalizable.

studies.authors: Joel Huber; John W. Payne; Christopher Puto
studies.title: Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives: Violations of Regularity and the Similarity Hypothesis
studies.finding: Adding an asymmetrically dominated 'decoy' — an option clearly inferior to a target but not to a competitor — raises the target's choice share by roughly 9 percentage points on average, violating the regularity axiom; the foundational demonstration of the attraction/decoy effect in consumer choice.
studies.groundsHow: Grounds menu anchoring — seating a deliberately dominated price/size next to a target to lift the target's share within a price band; we treat it as a real but stylized lever whose pull shrinks on realistic, multi-attribute menus.
studies.myth: Corrects two errors: crediting the decoy effect to Ariely/Poundstone popularizations (the primary source is Huber, Payne & Puto 1982), and treating it as a large universal lever — the ~9pp shift is robust in simple two-attribute lab choices but attenuates with complex real products and expert buyers.

studies.authors: Manoj Thomas; Vicki Morwitz
studies.title: Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition
studies.finding: Across five experiments, a 9-ending price ($2.99) is judged meaningfully smaller than a price one cent higher ($3.00) only when the leftmost digit changes; the bias is a left-digit anchoring effect in magnitude encoding, not a property of the '9' ending itself, and it strengthens as the compared prices get closer.
studies.groundsHow: Grounds price-threshold banding: the printed cents only bite at a left-digit break, so a posture landing near a whole-dollar line should be set just under it (e.g., 14.xx below 15) rather than reflexively appending '.99' everywhere.
studies.myth: Corrects the folk 'charm pricing — always end in 9 to read cheaper' rule: the effect requires the left digit to drop ($2.99 vs $3.00); $2.99 vs $2.89, sharing the same left digit, shows no such magnitude bias, so a 9-ending inside the same dollar buys nothing.

studies.authors: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food and Nutrition Service
studies.title: Food Buying Guide for Child Nutrition Programs (interactive web-based edition)
studies.venue: USDA Food and Nutrition Service — continuously updated online resource (updated for the 2024 final rule aligning Child Nutrition meal patterns with the 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines)
studies.finding: Publishes standardized as-purchased (AP) to served/edible-portion yield data in a six-column table (Column 1 Food As Purchased; Column 3 Servings per Purchase Unit, EP; Column 5 Purchase Units for 100 Servings; Column 6 Additional Yield Information) so an operator can calculate the AP quantity to buy to net a required amount of served food. It is the USDA's standardized, continuously-updated purchase-yield reference for Child Nutrition Programs, and is widely used beyond schools as a government foodservice purchase-yield reference.
studies.groundsHow: Our trim-tax multiplier (1 / edible yield) uses FBG-style AP-to-served yield factors as its standardized, citable basis; we extend the FBG's purchase-quantity math into a per-dollar cost penalty applied when pricing a menu item.
studies.myth: Corrects the assumption that the FBG is only for school/CACFP kitchens: its title scopes it to Child Nutrition Programs, but the underlying AP-to-served yield tables are a general USDA purchase-yield reference usable by any foodservice operator.

studies.authors: Pecot, Rebecca K.; Watt, Bernice K. (U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service)
studies.title: Food Yields Summarized by Different Stages of Preparation (Agriculture Handbook No. 102)
studies.venue: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agriculture Handbook No. 102 (orig. 1956; rev. 1975)
studies.finding: Compiles empirical percentage yields for a wide range of foods across successive preparation stages (as-purchased to trimmed/edible to cooked), quantifying refuse/trim losses and cooking losses relative to as-purchased weight.
studies.groundsHow: It is the primary empirical foundation the trim-tax rests on — documenting that edible yield after trim and cooking is materially below purchased weight; we convert those measured loss fractions into the 1/yield cost markup.
studies.myth: Many circulating 'edible-yield %' charts have no cited provenance; AH-102 is the actual primary USDA source those yield figures trace back to, not vendor lore.

studies.authors: Roseland, Janet M.; Nguyen, Quynh Anh; Williams, Juhi R.; Patterson, Kristine Y.; Showell, Bethany A.; Pehrsson, Pamela R. (USDA Agricultural Research Service)
studies.title: USDA Table of Cooking Yields for Meat and Poultry, Release 2
studies.venue: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Ag Data Commons dataset
studies.finding: Reports measured cooking yields (weight change from moisture and fat loss) for specific meat and poultry cuts under standardized cooking protocols, isolating cooking loss as a distinct component of edible yield separate from knife trim.
studies.groundsHow: Supplies the cooking-loss component of edible yield for proteins specifically; we use it to justify splitting the trim-tax into a trim component and a cook component rather than a single blended factor.
studies.myth: Corrects the belief that AP-to-EP yield loss is mostly knife trimming: for cooked proteins a large share of weight loss is moisture and fat driven off during cooking, not trim.

studies.authors: Dopson, Lea R.; Hayes, David K.
studies.title: Food and Beverage Cost Control, 7th Edition (Ch. 5, Monitoring Food and Beverage Product Costs)
studies.finding: Codifies the AP/EP framework and the yield test (butcher's/cooking test): the test produces a yield percentage, and edible-portion (servable) cost equals the as-purchased cost divided by that yield percentage — i.e., a cost factor of 1 divided by yield applied to the AP price.
studies.groundsHow: This is the canonical textbook statement of our trim-tax formula; our layer applies its cost factor (1 / yield %) as the multiplier on ingredient cost when costing and pricing a menu item.

studies.authors: Sam Peltzman
studies.title: Prices Rise Faster than They Fall
studies.venue: Journal of Political Economy (University of Chicago Press), 108(3), 466-502
studies.finding: Across 242 markets (77 consumer and 165 producer goods), output prices respond faster to input-cost increases than to decreases in more than two of every three markets, with the immediate response to a positive cost shock at least twice the response to an equal negative shock and the gap persisting five to eight months — the foundational cross-market demonstration of asymmetric 'rockets and feathers' pass-through.
studies.groundsHow: Our wholesale-reference bands are framed as market context rather than a live retail price precisely because Peltzman shows output prices track input costs up fast but down slowly, so a wholesale dip has not necessarily flowed through to what an operator actually pays.
studies.myth: Corrects the assumption that when wholesale or input costs fall, retail prices fall just as fast as they rose — Peltzman documents the opposite (rise-faster-than-fall) in roughly two-thirds of markets.

studies.authors: Jochen Meyer and Stephan von Cramon-Taubadel
studies.title: Asymmetric Price Transmission: A Survey
studies.finding: This agricultural-economics survey classifies the types, causes, and econometric measurement of asymmetric price transmission along farm-wholesale-retail chains, documenting that asymmetry is widespread empirically but arises from multiple mechanisms (adjustment/menu costs, inventory holding, search costs, and market power) rather than any single cause, and that measured asymmetry is sensitive to model specification and data frequency.
studies.groundsHow: We treat the farm-to-wholesale-to-retail chain as loosely and asymmetrically coupled per this survey, which is why our bands report a wholesale reference range rather than imputing a retail price from a wholesale move.
studies.myth: Corrects the myth that asymmetric pass-through is proof of seller collusion or retail market power — the survey shows asymmetry also arises from non-collusive mechanisms (menu/adjustment costs, inventory, search) and appears even in competitive settings.

studies.authors: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Economic Research Service (ERS)
studies.title: Food Dollar Series (farm share of the U.S. food dollar; companion: Price Spreads from Farm to Consumer)
studies.venue: USDA Economic Research Service (ERS) data product
studies.finding: In the U.S. food-dollar accounting, farm establishments received about 15.9 cents of each dollar U.S. consumers spent on domestically produced food in 2023 (the 'farm share'), with the large majority going to post-farm marketing costs — processing, packaging, transportation, wholesaling, and retailing; the companion Price Spreads from Farm to Consumer series (a distinct ERS data product) reports farm value, wholesale, and retail values whose spreads move partly independently of farm-gate prices.
studies.groundsHow: Our 'wholesale is not what you pay' honesty rests directly on this official accounting: because the farm/commodity value is a minority (~16 cents) of the retail food dollar, a commodity or wholesale move cannot be read one-to-one into an operator's menu cost.
studies.myth: Corrects the folk belief that the farm/commodity (or wholesale) price is most of what you pay and that farmers capture most of the food dollar — the 2023 farm share is about 15.9 cents; the majority is post-farm marketing cost.

studies.authors: Holbrook Working
studies.title: The Theory of Price of Storage
studies.venue: The American Economic Review (American Economic Association), vol. 39, no. 6, pp. 1254-1262
studies.finding: Working demonstrated that the price relationship between a commodity for delivery at different dates (the intertemporal or 'storage' spread) is set by the quantity of supply currently on hand and the competitively-determined cost of carrying it forward, not by the market's expectation of future price change—so the recurring harvest-glut-to-lean-season price structure is the return earned for storing supply across time.
studies.groundsHow: This underwrites why a seasonal window exists at all—storage arbitrage smooths but cannot erase the glut-to-lean cost cycle—while cautioning that the spread is a return to storage, not a forecast, which is exactly why our seasonal-window layer prices around a recurring shape and never forecasts a level.
studies.myth: Corrects the common belief that a forward/seasonal price gap is the market 'predicting' future scarcity; Working shows the spread reflects current supply and carrying cost, so it is not a price forecast to be traded on.

studies.authors: Robert B. Cleveland, William S. Cleveland, Jean E. McRae, and Irma Terpenning
studies.title: STL: A Seasonal-Trend Decomposition Procedure Based on Loess (with Discussion)
studies.venue: Journal of Official Statistics (Statistics Sweden), vol. 6, no. 1, pp. 3-73
studies.finding: Cleveland, Cleveland, McRae and Terpenning introduced STL, a robust loess-based procedure that splits a time series into trend, a seasonal component allowed to evolve gradually over time, and a remainder, giving a resistant way to estimate the recurring seasonal shape without a single anomalous observation distorting it.
studies.groundsHow: Our seasonal-window layer estimates each ingredient's recurring shape in the STL spirit—decomposing a price history into trend + seasonal + remainder with a robust, time-varying seasonal component—so an outlier week does not redraw the window and a slowly-shifting season is still captured.

studies.authors: David F. Findley, Brian C. Monsell, William R. Bell, Mark C. Otto, and Bor-Chung Chen
studies.title: New Capabilities and Methods of the X-12-ARIMA Seasonal-Adjustment Program
studies.venue: Journal of Business & Economic Statistics (American Statistical Association / Taylor & Francis), vol. 16, no. 2, pp. 127-152
studies.finding: Documenting the U.S. Census Bureau's X-12-ARIMA program, the authors describe its seasonal-adjustment method and diagnostic suite, including the tests used to decide whether a series' seasonal movement is statistically identifiable (the combined stable-plus-moving F-tests and Kruskal-Wallis test, after Lothian and Morry) rather than a series that merely looks seasonal.
studies.groundsHow: Our noise gate operationalizes the same principle these diagnostics formalize: a seasonal window is drawn only when the recurring component is large and stable relative to the remainder, so scatter is never promoted to a 'season'—we require identifiable seasonality before publishing a window.
studies.myth: Corrects the myth that any recurring dip or peak is 'seasonal'; the identifiable-seasonality framework this program reports shows apparent patterns can fail the stable/moving/nonparametric tests and must be treated as non-seasonal noise.

studies.authors: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Economic Research Service
studies.title: Starchy fresh vegetables (excluding potatoes) had the most seasonal price variation from 2016-18 (Charts of Note, from Food-at-Home Monthly Area Prices data)
studies.finding: Using Food-at-Home Monthly Area Prices for 2016-18, USDA ERS found that seasonal price variation among fresh vegetables is category- and item-specific: it is largest for the 'other starchy vegetables' group (dominated by sweet corn), which is cheapest in summer when domestic supply peaks, and smallest for dark green vegetables, which show little seasonal price movement.
studies.groundsHow: This grounds our per-ingredient (not blanket) seasonal windows: because seasonality varies by category and item, we estimate a window for each ingredient rather than assuming a uniform 'summer is cheap' rule, and we suppress windows for low-variation items like dark greens.
studies.myth: Corrects the 'all produce is cheapest in summer / produce is uniformly seasonal' oversimplification; ERS shows some categories have pronounced summer troughs while others (dark greens) show minimal seasonal price variation.

studies.authors: Angus Deaton; John Muellbauer
studies.title: An Almost Ideal Demand System
studies.finding: Introduced the Almost Ideal Demand System (AIDS), a theoretically consistent demand model in which each good's budget share is linear in log prices and log real expenditure, yielding estimable own-price, cross-price, and expenditure elasticities and permitting direct tests of homogeneity and symmetry.
studies.groundsHow: It is the demand-system backbone our substitution finder rests on: substitutability is a property of estimated compensated demand response, so we treat 'substitute' as a demand-model claim, never a raw price-correlation claim.

studies.authors: Abigail M. Okrent; Julian M. Alston
studies.title: The Demand for Disaggregated Food-Away-from-Home and Food-at-Home Products in the United States
studies.venue: USDA Economic Research Service, Economic Research Report No. 139 (ERR-139)
studies.finding: Estimating a demand system for 43 disaggregated food-away-from-home and food-at-home products in the United States via two-stage budgeting, they recover own-price, expenditure, and cross-price elasticities and find many statistically significant substitution and complementary relationships within and across food categories, with food-away-from-home items being expenditure-elastic 'luxuries.'
studies.groundsHow: It supplies real U.S. food cross-price elasticities showing substitution is pair- and category-specific and frequently small, so our finder derives a candidate swap's hedging value from measured demand response rather than assuming any two ingredients substitute.

studies.authors: Robert S. Pindyck; Julio J. Rotemberg
studies.title: The Excess Co-Movement of Commodity Prices
studies.finding: Prices of largely unrelated raw commodities (wheat, cotton, copper, gold, crude oil, lumber, cocoa) exhibit persistent co-movement well in excess of anything that common macroeconomic fundamentals - inflation, industrial production, interest rates, and exchange rates - can explain.
studies.groundsHow: It is the empirical warrant for our core honesty rule - that two ingredients whose wholesale prices move together are not thereby substitutes and swapping one for the other does not hedge - because co-movement is driven by shared macro/financial forces, not by any demand relationship between the goods (we flag that later work, e.g. Deb-Trivedi-Varangis 1996, contests the magnitude of the 'excess,' though not that unrelated commodities co-move).
studies.myth: The myth that price co-movement reveals an economic linkage - that co-moving goods are substitutes/complements, or that a co-moving swap hedges; Pindyck-Rotemberg show commodity-price co-movement exceeds and is unexplained by common fundamentals, so co-movement is not evidence of substitutability.

studies.authors: Tatiana Andreyeva; Michael W. Long; Kelly D. Brownell
studies.title: The Impact of Food Prices on Consumption: A Systematic Review of Research on the Price Elasticity of Demand for Food
studies.finding: A systematic review of 160 studies found mean own-price elasticities of demand for major U.S. food and beverage categories clustering in the inelastic range (absolute values roughly 0.27 to 0.81), with food away from home, soft drinks, juice, and meats the most price-responsive (about 0.7-0.8) and eggs the least (about 0.27).
studies.groundsHow: It grounds the finder's category-specific humility: measured food price-responsiveness varies widely by category and robust cross-price/substitution estimates are comparatively scarce, so a proposed swap's hedging benefit must be evidenced per category rather than assumed from a single 'food is inelastic' rule of thumb.
studies.myth: The myth of a single or uniform food price elasticity (that 'food demand is inelastic' as one number); the review documents that elasticities differ substantially by category, with food away from home among the most price-responsive.

studies.authors: Austin Clowes, Craig Hanson, and Richard Swannell (on behalf of Champions 12.3)
studies.title: The Business Case for Reducing Food Loss and Waste: Restaurants
studies.venue: Champions 12.3, in partnership with the World Resources Institute (WRI) and WRAP
studies.finding: A study of 114 restaurant sites across 12 countries found nearly every site achieved a positive return, with the average restaurant saving about $7 for every $1 invested in cutting kitchen food waste; sites reduced waste roughly 26% within the first year, over 75% recouped their investment within a year (89% within two years), and every site kept total investment under $20,000.
studies.groundsHow: Our trim-to-value layer uses this restaurant-specific 7:1 as its conservative, real-world ROI anchor for turning measured trim and waste reduction into recovered margin, rather than leaning on the inflated cross-sector number.
studies.myth: The belief that kitchen food-waste programs demand heavy capital and have long paybacks - the study found every one of the 114 sites invested under $20,000 and most recouped within a single year.

studies.authors: Craig Hanson and Peter Mitchell (on behalf of Champions 12.3)
studies.title: The Business Case for Reducing Food Loss and Waste
studies.venue: Champions 12.3, in partnership with the World Resources Institute (WRI) and WRAP
studies.finding: Across 1,200 business sites in 700 companies spanning 17 countries, nearly every site achieved a positive return on food-loss-and-waste reduction, with half realizing a benefit-cost ratio of 14:1 or greater (an average of roughly $14 saved for every $1 invested).
studies.groundsHow: It grounds our why-it-matters case that measuring and acting on waste reliably pays back at scale, while our page deliberately cites the restaurant-specific 7:1 instead of this headline 14:1 to avoid overstating the return for a single kitchen.
studies.myth: The widely repeated '14:1 return on food-waste reduction' is a multi-sector average (manufacturing, retail, hospitality, foodservice) that is routinely mis-applied to restaurants specifically; the restaurant-only companion study puts the figure at about 7:1.

studies.authors: ReFED (Rethink Food Waste Through Economics and Data), a multi-stakeholder collaboration
studies.title: A Roadmap to Reduce U.S. Food Waste by 20 Percent
studies.finding: ReFED's first national economic analysis identified 27 cost-effective, scalable solutions that could cut US food waste about 20% (roughly 13 million tons per year) and generate about $100 billion in cumulative economic value over a decade, finding prevention far more economically valuable per ton than recycling and naming Waste Tracking & Analytics the single most economically valuable business-facing solution (an estimated $1.3 billion in gross annual business cost savings), with restaurants and foodservice positioned to capture the large majority of that prevention profit potential.
studies.groundsHow: It grounds the trim-to-value mechanism - that the highest-ROI lever is measuring and tracking waste before cutting it, and that restaurants and foodservice capture most of the resulting profit - which our layer frames as measure-then-trim.
studies.myth: The assumption that composting and recycling are the top food-waste levers - ReFED found prevention solutions such as waste tracking deliver far greater economic value per ton than recycling food scraps.

studies.authors: H. G. Parsa, John T. Self, David Njite, Tiffany King
studies.title: Why Restaurants Fail
studies.venue: Cornell Hotel and Restaurant Administration Quarterly, 46(3), 304-322 (SAGE)
studies.finding: Using Dun & Bradstreet longitudinal records for independent restaurants (Columbus, Ohio, 1996-1999), first-year failure was 26.16%, and cumulative three-year failure was roughly 57-61% (franchise chains 57.2%, independents 61.4%; the three-year cumulative rate did not exceed ~60%). A literature review found no empirical basis for the widely repeated 90%-fail-in-year-one claim, and failure was also traced to non-financial drivers, notably family life-cycle / quality-of-life management and, qualitatively, location.
studies.groundsHow: Our analysis stands on the corrected ~26% first-year figure (not 90%) to argue honestly that restaurant failure is real but survivable, so margin and per-ingredient cost control is a lever operators genuinely hold rather than a lost cause.
studies.myth: The 'about 90% of restaurants fail in their first year' claim: Parsa found it widely accepted with no data behind it and traced it to an American Express-linked source (the AmEx-sponsored reality show 'The Restaurant') that, when asked, stated in writing it could not provide supporting data. The peer-reviewed first-year rate for independents was ~26% (26.16%).

studies.authors: H. G. Parsa, John Self, Sandra Sydnor-Busso, Hae Jin Yoon
studies.title: Why Restaurants Fail? Part II - The Impact of Affiliation, Location, and Size on Restaurant Failures: Results from a Survival Analysis
studies.venue: Journal of Foodservice Business Research, 14(4), 360-379 (Taylor & Francis)
studies.finding: A survival (hazard) analysis of restaurant failures showing that mortality is systematically structured by affiliation (chain/multi-unit vs. independent), location (zip code), and size rather than random: independents faced substantially elevated closure risk versus chain-affiliated restaurants, and smaller restaurants failed at higher rates than larger ones.
studies.groundsHow: We extend this by treating the finding that independents carry structurally higher failure hazard as the reason their thinner cash buffers make disciplined per-ingredient costing a survival tool, not a nicety.

studies.authors: National Restaurant Association
studies.title: 2025 Restaurant Operations Report (Restaurant Operations Data Abstract)
studies.finding: Drawing on financial and operational data from more than 900 U.S. restaurants, the report shows fullservice restaurants had a median income before taxes of 2.8% of sales and limited-service restaurants 4.0%, documenting the industry's thin, low-single-digit net-margin structure.
studies.groundsHow: Our 'why cost discipline matters' layer rests on these low-single-digit median pre-tax margins: because the cushion is only a few points of sales, a small drift in food cost can erase an independent's entire profit, which is exactly why per-ingredient tracking matters.
studies.myth: The lay perception that restaurants are high-margin cash businesses; the authoritative operator benchmark shows median pre-tax margins in the low single digits (2.8% fullservice / 4.0% limited-service).

studies.authors: Tornberg, E.
studies.title: Effects of heat on meat proteins – Implications on structure and quality of meat products
studies.finding: A review of how heat restructures meat proteins. The globular sarcoplasmic and myofibrillar proteins begin to denature and aggregate around 40°C, with most set by about 60°C and coagulation continuing up to ~90°C; as this network denatures it shrinks and squeezes out held water, so cooking (water) loss rises with temperature. Collagen (connective tissue) denatures at roughly 53-63°C and its fibers shrink, and on continued moist heating the shrunken collagen dissolves into gelatin unless it is locked up by heat-stable crosslinks.
studies.kitchen: The hotter you take a cut, the more water its proteins wring out and the less it weighs on the plate — that is your cooked yield falling as doneness climbs, so a well-done steak gives up clearly more moisture than one pulled at medium-rare. Connective-tissue-heavy cuts are the opposite bet: hold them hot and wet long enough and the collagen that made them tough melts to gelatin, which is exactly why a chuck or shank must be cooked far past the point that would ruin a loin.

studies.authors: Palka, K., & Daun, H.
studies.title: Changes in texture, cooking losses, and myofibrillar structure of bovine M. semitendinosus during heating
studies.finding: Slices of beef semitendinosus (eye of round) were cooked to internal temperatures from 50 up to 121°C. Cooking losses rose progressively as temperature increased, the myofibrils shrank in diameter and sarcomere length, and texture-profile toughness increased, with the toughening tied to changes in the myofibrillar proteins above roughly 70°C.
studies.kitchen: This is your shrink curve measured in a lab: every extra degree of doneness costs weight and plate size, and much of the water dumps early as the meat sets. Portioning a roast for well-done guests means buying more raw ounces per finished portion than for a rare service, so build the doneness you actually serve into your cost per cover — not just the raw price on the invoice.

studies.authors: Christensen, M., Purslow, P. P., & Larsen, L. M.
studies.title: The effect of cooking temperature on mechanical properties of whole meat, single muscle fibres and perimysial connective tissue
studies.finding: In beef, whole-meat toughness rose in two separate phases as cooking temperature climbed: once from about 40-50°C, driven by changes in the perimysial connective tissue (collagen), and again from 60-80°C, driven by the muscle fibers themselves getting stronger — with a dip in toughness between 50 and 60°C. Below 60°C the connective tissue governs toughness; above 60°C the muscle fibers do.
studies.kitchen: Toughness has two different causes at two different temperatures, which is why 'just cook it longer' backfires on the wrong cut. Past medium the muscle fibers tighten and toughen (bad news for a lean loin), while the collagen problem in a cheap, sinewy cut only surrenders under long, wet, hot cooking. Match the method to the enemy: fast and gentle for tender cuts, low-and-slow braise for connective-tissue cuts — one method cannot serve both.

studies.authors: Dashdorj, D., Tripathi, V. K., Cho, S., Kim, Y., & Hwang, I.
studies.title: Dry aging of beef; Review
studies.venue: Journal of Animal Science and Technology
studies.finding: A review of beef dry-aging. Holding primals in controlled cold, humid, moving air for weeks dehydrates the surface: moisture evaporates and a hard crust (pellicle) forms. Reported weight shrinkage runs about 6-15%, and the dried, inedible crust trimmed off afterward removes another 3-24%, so total loss before sale can approach roughly 30-40% of what was bought.
studies.kitchen: Dry-aging is a yield tax you pay for flavor. Between water that simply evaporates (6-15%) and the dried crust you trim away (up to ~24%), you can lose a third or more of the purchase weight as sellable meat — so a dry-aged steak has to be menu-priced off the trimmed, aged weight, never the raw buy weight, or the program bleeds margin quietly on every plate.

studies.authors: Susana C. Fonseca, Fernanda A. R. Oliveira, Jeffrey K. Brecht
studies.title: Modelling respiration rate of fresh fruits and vegetables for modified atmosphere packages: a review
studies.finding: Respiration is a harvested plant's living metabolism: it keeps burning its own stored sugars and acids, consuming oxygen and giving off CO2, until its reserves run down and it senesces. This review compiles the measured data and models showing respiration rate is the master variable for storage life, and that the rate rises steeply with temperature (roughly a two- to fourfold increase per 10 degrees C, the Q10 effect) as well as with injury and maturity. Higher-respiring commodities (leafy greens, herbs, mushrooms, broccoli, sweet corn, peas, asparagus) deteriorate fastest; low-respiring ones (onions, potatoes, apples, mature roots) hold longest.
studies.kitchen: A crate of produce is literally eating itself, and heat is the throttle. Every 10 degrees C (about 18 F) warmer roughly doubles or more the rate it burns down, so a case left on a summer dock for two hours ages like most of a day in the walk-in. That is the whole reason cold storage works, and the reason to move deliveries off the dock into the cooler immediately. It also tells you what to buy short: high-respiration items (greens, herbs, mushrooms, broccoli, corn, peas, asparagus) burn hottest and die first, so buy them close to service; roots, onions, potatoes, and apples tolerate long holds.

studies.authors: Mikal E. Saltveit
studies.title: Effect of ethylene on quality of fresh fruits and vegetables
studies.finding: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone. Climacteric fruits (tomato, banana, apple, avocado, pear, melon, stone fruit) emit a burst of it and use it to trigger their own ripening; many other commodities do not make much but are highly sensitive to it. This review catalogs how even trace ethylene in the air accelerates ripening and senescence in sensitive produce: softening, yellowing of green vegetables, russet-spotting and bitterness in carrots, toughening of asparagus, and faster overall breakdown. It covers both the deliberate use of ethylene to ripen and the damage from unwanted exposure, plus how to manage it.
studies.kitchen: Some fruit gasses off a ripening signal that ages everything parked near it. Keep the ethylene producers (apples, bananas, tomatoes, avocados, melons, pears, stone fruit) out of the same reach-in as your ethylene-sensitive product (leafy greens, herbs, broccoli, cucumbers, carrots) or the banana box will yellow your lettuce and turn carrots bitter days early. That mystery of a whole herb lowboy dying in two days is often an ethylene producer sitting next to it. Flip it when you want to: bag hard avocados or tomatoes with a banana at room temp overnight to have them ripe for tomorrow's service.

studies.authors: Bo Zhang, Denise M. Tieman, Chen Jiao, Yimin Xu, Kunsong Chen, Zhangjun Fei, James J. Giovannoni, Harry J. Klee
studies.title: Chilling-induced tomato flavor loss is associated with altered volatile synthesis and transient changes in DNA methylation
studies.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), 113(44), 12580-12585
studies.finding: Holding ripe tomatoes at refrigerator temperatures (the study chilled at 5 degrees C; flavor volatiles are sensitive below about 12 degrees C) shuts down the genes that build the aroma compounds responsible for tomato flavor. A 76-person taste panel rated chilled tomatoes as significantly blander than unchilled fruit, and the researchers showed that some of the switched-off flavor genes did not fully recover even after the tomatoes were rewarmed to 20 degrees C. This is chilling injury expressed as largely permanent flavor loss, distinct from softening or texture damage.
studies.kitchen: The fridge murders tomato flavor, and it does not fully come back on the counter. Hold ripe tomatoes at room temperature or in a cool pantry around 55 F, not in the walk-in. If tomatoes arrive cold or you have to refrigerate a surplus to avoid losing them, treat that as trading flavor for a few days of hold: send the cold-held fruit to cooked uses (sauce, roasted, braises) where aroma matters less, and reserve unchilled tomatoes for anything raw, caprese, slicing, salsa, salad, where flavor is the product.

studies.authors: J. E. Robinson, K. M. Browne, W. G. Burton
studies.title: Storage characteristics of some vegetables and soft fruits
studies.finding: This classic study measured how much weight (essentially water, lost through transpiration) a range of vegetables and soft fruits can shed before they wilt or shrivel enough to be unsaleable, producing the maximum-permissible-weight-loss figures still cited in postharvest handbooks today. Leafy vegetables such as lettuce were rated unacceptable after only about 3 to 5 percent weight loss, green peppers around 7 percent, with sturdier items tolerating more. The key point is that water loss, not microbial decay, is frequently the first thing that renders fresh produce unsellable.
studies.kitchen: Produce usually becomes trim before it ever becomes rot; it wilts. Leafy greens and herbs only need to lose 3 to 5 percent of their weight to look limp and get pulled, meaning the case shrinks and you are paying by the pound for yield you cannot plate. Fight it: keep the walk-in humid, do not store greens in the dry blast right in front of the evaporator fan, keep product covered, wrapped, or in liners, and do not hold washed greens loose and exposed. The wilt you toss midweek from Monday's delivery is water weight you bought, so size leafy and herb orders to your real turn rate.

studies.authors: Qian, S., Hu, F., Mehmood, W., Li, X., Zhang, C., & Blecker, C.
studies.title: The rise of thawing drip: Freezing rate effects on ice crystallization and myowater dynamics changes
studies.finding: In beef loin (bovine longissimus), how fast the meat freezes controls both ice-crystal size and where the water ends up. Ultra-fast freezing formed many small, uniformly sized ice crystals (a narrow size distribution) and kept water bound inside the muscle structure; slow freezing let a few large crystals grow, which physically disrupted the tissue and shifted water from the protein-held (immobilized) state into 'free' water — exactly what runs out as thaw drip (about 4.35% loss under ultra-fast vs 8.22% under slow freezing). Faster freezing also better preserved the myofibrillar proteins (higher solubility, more stable structure), so slower freezing meant both more thaw drip and more protein damage.
studies.kitchen: The speed a cut hits solid-frozen decides how much liquid it bleeds when you thaw it — and that purge is weight you already paid for and yield you'll never plate. A warm cut shoved into a packed freezer freezes slowly, grows big crystals that shred the muscle, and pools purge on the board. Freeze protein in a single layer with air around each piece (or use a blast/quick-freeze setup); don't stack warm cuts into a full deep bin. Small, fast-frozen portions thaw back closest to fresh weight.

studies.authors: Ngapo, T. M., Babare, I. H., Reynolds, J., & Mawson, R. F.
studies.title: Freezing and thawing rate effects on drip loss from samples of pork
studies.finding: Testing six freezing rates, two storage times, and three thawing rates on small (~6 g) pork samples — with drip collected by centrifugal extraction and protein denaturation tracked by differential scanning calorimetry — fast freezing produced drip loss that was not significantly different from never-frozen fresh meat, while slow freezing produced clearly more drip. After four weeks of frozen storage, drip loss at the slow freezing rates grew significantly larger than in unstored samples, eroding the fast-freeze advantage. (The study also varied thawing rate, but its thawing-rate effects were mixed and condition-dependent rather than a single clean optimum.)
studies.kitchen: Two things you control. First, freeze fast — thin and spread out — so pork thaws back to near-fresh weight instead of leaking purge into the pan; a slow freeze in a packed bin costs you drip you already paid for. Second, don't treat the freezer as a vault: even a well-frozen cut gives up more purge the longer it sits, so date every bag and rotate oldest-first rather than hoard frozen protein. Cost a long-held frozen cut knowing it plates a bit lighter than its raw weight — a real gap on a high-volume line.

studies.authors: Lee, C. Y., Smith, N. L., & Hawbecker, D. E.
studies.title: Enzyme activity and quality of frozen green beans as affected by blanching and storage
studies.finding: Green beans were blanched at a range of temperature/time combinations, frozen, and held at -23 degrees C for up to 12 months, then scored for residual enzyme activity, sensory quality, color, and firmness at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. A hotter, more complete blanch (above about 82 degrees C for 3.5 min) knocked down the quality-wrecking enzymes (peroxidase, lipoxygenase, polyphenoloxidase, catalase) and scored higher for taste, color, and firmness after storage than under-blanched beans. Under-blanching leaves those enzymes active, and they keep degrading color, flavor, and texture even at freezer temperatures.
studies.kitchen: Freezing pauses microbes but not the vegetable's own enzymes — an unblanched green bean or pea keeps going dull, off-flavored, and limp in your freezer over the months. A quick hard blanch (rolling-boil dunk, then straight into an ice bath) before you freeze produce is what buys a year of good color and snap instead of a faded, mushy bag by month three. Skip the blanch and you're freezing a clock that's still ticking. Applies to vegetables you prep and freeze yourself, not proteins.

studies.authors: Teuteberg, V., Kluth, I.-K., Ploetz, M., & Krischek, C.
studies.title: Effects of duration and temperature of frozen storage on the quality and food safety characteristics of pork after thawing and after storage under modified atmosphere
studies.finding: Pork was frozen for 12 vs 24 weeks at either -18 degrees C or -80 degrees C, then thawed and tracked in modified-atmosphere packs for up to 14 days. Freezing-and-thawing raised total moisture (drip plus storage) loss versus never-frozen pork, and longer frozen storage (24 weeks) worsened outcomes — including pigment changes (more metmyoglobin/browning, less oxymyoglobin) tied to reduced consumer acceptance. Notably, ultra-cold -80 degrees C storage did not significantly outperform an ordinary -18 degrees C freezer — time in the freezer mattered more than chasing a colder temperature.
studies.kitchen: A frozen cut is never quite a fresh cut — it comes back lighter, having surrendered purge, and the longer it sat frozen the more it gives up and the browner/less appealing it looks once thawed. Practical read: your standard -18 degrees C freezer is fine, there's no yield to buy by going colder; the lever that matters is time-in-freezer. Date every bag, use oldest first, and cost frozen protein knowing a long-held cut plates a bit lighter than its raw weight — a real gap on a high-volume line.

studies.authors: T. L. Potter and I. S. Fagerson
studies.title: Composition of coriander leaf volatiles
studies.venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 38(11), 2054–2056
studies.finding: The characteristic smell of fresh cilantro (coriander) leaf comes overwhelmingly from a family of long-chain aliphatic aldehydes — chiefly (E)-2-decenal and decanal, alongside other C10–C16 2-alkenals and n-alkanals. In this study these aldehydes were the dominant volatiles isolated from the leaf, and they are what the nose reads as 'cilantro.'
studies.kitchen: Cilantro's flavor lives in a specific set of aldehyde molecules that no other common herb on your line carries in the same combination. That's why swapping in parsley or reaching for 'a little more lime' never actually reads as cilantro — you can match the green color and the fresh look, but not the aldehyde signature. If a plate is built on cilantro, treat it as non-substitutable for flavor: 86 it or re-spec the dish, don't fake it. It also explains why cilantro fades fast once chopped and heated — those volatile aldehydes cook off — so add it late and raw.

studies.authors: Y. Qiao, B. J. Xie, Yan Zhang, Yun Zhang, G. Fan, X. L. Yao, and S. Y. Pan
studies.title: Characterization of Aroma Active Compounds in Fruit Juice and Peel Oil of Jinchen Sweet Orange Fruit (Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck) by GC-MS and GC-O
studies.finding: Using sniff-port gas chromatography (GC-O) plus GC-MS, the researchers showed that an orange's juice and its peel oil are two different aroma sources. Of the 41 aroma-active compounds detected across both fractions, only 12 were shared; the juice was dominated by esters and aldehydes (e.g., ethyl butanoate, octanal) while the peel oil — pressed from the flavedo, the colored outer skin — was dominated by terpenes and terpene alcohols (e.g., β-myrcene, α-pinene, linalool). The two fractions smell distinct because they are chemically distinct (49 total compounds identified in juice vs. 32 in peel oil).
studies.kitchen: The bright, 'orange-y' top note you want for a garnish is in the peel oil, not the juice — the flavedo (colored zest layer) is the concentrated aroma source, and the juice carries a different, softer profile. Practical calls: for aromatic lift, zest or express the peel over the plate or drink; don't expect juice to deliver it, and don't expect zest to replace the body and acid juice gives. It also means the two aren't interchangeable on a spec sheet — 'we're out of fresh oranges, use bottled juice' throws away the entire peel-oil aroma set. When the peel is doing the flavor work, buy whole fruit; the yield you're really paying for is the zest, so plan garnish counts around fruit you can peel, not just ounces of juice.

studies.authors: S. I. F. S. Martins, W. M. F. Jongen, and M. A. J. S. van Boekel
studies.title: A review of Maillard reaction in food and implications to kinetic modelling
studies.finding: The Maillard reaction is the heat-driven cascade between amino acids (from protein) and reducing sugars that produces both browning and hundreds of new aroma compounds that were not present in the raw ingredient. This review shows the reaction is governed by heat, time, moisture, and pH, and that the color, flavor, and nutritional changes it drives are coupled and can be described with kinetic (multiresponse) modelling from those conditions — it is flavor you build with cooking, not flavor that was already there.
studies.kitchen: The roasty, savory flavor of a seared steak crust, caramelized onions, toasted bread, or dark-roast coffee is manufactured by cooking — those compounds simply don't exist in the raw product. That's why a boiled or steamed version of the same ingredient never tastes like the browned one, and why a raw or under-caramelized substitute falls flat. On the line it means dry the surface, don't crowd the pan, and give it real heat and time: you're not just cooking the item, you're generating flavor that carries menu value. It also caps shortcuts — you can't skip the sear and buy the flavor back with more salt or a splash of sauce.

studies.authors: W. Grosch
studies.title: Evaluation of the Key Odorants of Foods by Dilution Experiments, Aroma Models and Omission
studies.finding: Across foods as different as coffee, boiled beef, olive oil, wine, and French fries, a food's characteristic aroma is carried by a surprisingly small set of 'key odorants.' When researchers rebuild the aroma from pure compounds (an aroma model) and then leave one compound out (an omission test), the smell noticeably shifts — direct proof that a handful of specific molecules are load-bearing for the food's identity. The review notes odorants with higher odour activity values are usually essential, with some exceptions.
studies.kitchen: A dish's signature smell hangs on a few specific molecules, not on 'roughly similar' ingredients. That's the hard, mechanistic reason a substitution is never a perfect match: if the swap doesn't carry the same key odorants, the guest's nose registers that something is off even if they can't name it. Use it as a decision rule — when you sub an ingredient, ask whether it actually delivers the one or two compounds that define the original (the sear, the citrus peel oil, the specific herb). If it doesn't, change how the dish is framed rather than pretending it's the same, and reserve the real ingredient for the plates where it's genuinely doing the work.

studies.authors: Weatherly, B.H.; Griffin, D.B.; Johnson, H.K.; Walter, J.P.; De La Zerda, M.J.; Tipton, N.C.; Savell, J.W.
studies.title: Foodservice yield and fabrication times for beef as influenced by purchasing options and merchandising styles
studies.finding: Professional cutters at three foodservice purveyors fabricated beef subprimals into ready-to-cook portion cuts while researchers weighed every cut and timed every job. Both the total usable yield and the labor time depended on the cutting spec, and the two moved against each other: as the target steak size got smaller, more steaks came off a given subprimal, but total foodservice yield fell and total cutting time rose — an inverse relationship between how much usable product you kept and how long the cutting took.
studies.kitchen: When you buy a subprimal (a whole strip loin, ribeye, or tenderloin) and cut your own steaks, two costs push against you at once: trimming closer and portioning smaller loses more to trim AND burns more butcher minutes. The low per-pound subprimal price is not your real cost — figure true plate cost on the yielded, cut weight plus the labor clock. A looser portion spec, or buying one step closer to portion-ready, can pencil out cheaper than full in-house breakdown once labor is counted.

studies.authors: Purslow, P.P.; Oiseth, S.; Hughes, J.; Warner, R.D.
studies.title: The structural basis of cooking loss in beef: Variations with temperature and ageing
studies.finding: In aged beef eye-of-round (semitendinosus), the water squeezed out during cooking comes mainly from the muscle fibers themselves shrinking, not from connective tissue. Fibers shrink sideways (cross-sectional area down about 20-24%) as myosin denatures around 50-65 C, then shrink lengthwise as actin denatures around 70-75 C — so cooking loss climbs in two temperature-driven steps as the center gets hotter. Meat aged longer (14 days vs 1 day) gave up more fluid when cooked.
studies.kitchen: Cooking shrink is not one flat percentage — it is driven by how hot you take the center, in steps. Pushing a steak from medium-rare up toward well-done crosses a second wave of water loss, leaving a smaller, lighter portion on the plate; well-done tickets literally shrink more product than rare ones. If you spec a cooked or served weight, the doneness you cook to changes your yield and your cost per plate. And a longer-aged cut, though more tender, can shed a bit more moisture in the pan — worth knowing when you plate to a target weight.

studies.authors: Hudspeth, J.P.; Lyon, C.E.; Lyon, B.G.; Mercuri, A.J.
studies.title: Weights of broiler parts as related to carcass weights and type of cut
studies.finding: Across 960 broiler carcasses spanning a wide weight range (under 450 g to 2000 g), cut into parts eight different commercial ways, each named part held a remarkably stable share of the whole carcass regardless of bird size — roughly 17% for a split breast-with-back down to about 5% for a drumstick portion. A single average percentage per cut predicted piece weight well across all sizes, and predictions were most reliable when the cut followed a joint or other clear anatomical landmark.
studies.kitchen: When you break down whole birds, each part is a predictable slice of the whole, so you can cost a whole chicken by the parts you actually sell before you pick up the knife. If your menu features only breasts (about a fifth of the carcass) or only thighs, the rest is trim you either resell (stock, staff meal, ground) or eat as loss — whole-bird price per pound badly overstates the value of the one part you plate. Because the part percentages hold across bird sizes, one yield table covers your whole size range, and cutting cleanly through the joint gives the most consistent portions.

studies.authors: Okomoda, V.T.; Solomon, S.G.; Wukatda, S.S.; Ikape, S.I.; Ikhwanuddin, M.; Abol-Munafi, A.B.
studies.title: Fillet Yield and Length-Weight Relationship of Five Fish Species From Lower River Benue, Makurdi, Nigeria
studies.finding: Filleting 60 fish each of five species, researchers found edible/fillet yield swung widely by species: three species (Mormyrus rume, Labeo senegalensis, and the catfish Clarias gariepinus) yielded at least 55% edible parts, while the other two yielded 39% or less. For most species the yield percentage stayed roughly constant regardless of fish size; only the catfish yield rose with larger fish.
studies.kitchen: With whole fish, the species — not the sticker price — decides how much you actually plate. Two whole fish at the same price per pound can hand you very different edible pounds: one might fillet out at over half its weight, another under 40%, so the 'cheaper' fish can cost more per usable ounce once you account for head, frame, and skin. Always convert whole-fish AP price to a per-fillet-pound (EP) cost using that species' real dress-out — and since yield mostly does not change with fish size, one yield figure per species holds across the sizes you buy.

studies.authors: Turhan, M.; Sayar, S.; Gunasekaran, S.
studies.title: Application of Peleg model to study water absorption in chickpea during soaking
studies.finding: Soaking dried chickpeas follows a predictable curve: water rushes in fast at first, then the uptake rate tapers as the seed nears saturation. The authors showed the two-constant Peleg equation reproduces this entire soaking curve — for five winter- and five spring-planted chickpea genotypes across water temperatures from 20 to 100 C — using only early-timepoint data, and that warmer soak water hydrates faster (the model's equilibrium form estimates the fully-hydrated endpoint at temperatures at or above 40 C). A soaked-out chickpea has taken on roughly its own dry weight in water.
studies.kitchen: Dried chickpeas roughly double in weight by the time they're soaked, so a pound of dry garbanzos becomes about two pounds hydrated before they ever hit the pot — that swell is your real yield behind the low dry price on the invoice. Most of the water goes in during the first few hours, so an overnight soak is plenty; you gain little past that. If you're behind, a hot soak gets you fully hydrated faster than a cold one.

studies.authors: Zamindar, N.; Baghekhandan, M. S.; Nasirpour, A.; et al.
studies.title: Effect of line, soaking and cooking time on water absorption, texture and splitting of red kidney beans
studies.venue: Journal of Food Science and Technology, 50(1), 108-114
studies.finding: Testing several Iranian red kidney bean lines, the authors found that how much water a bean absorbs, how tender it cooks, and how much it splits all depend on three factors: the bean line (variety/genetics), the soaking time, and the cooking time. Longer soaking raised water absorption and shortened cooking time, and some lines absorbed markedly more water than others under identical conditions — the D81083 line absorbed the most after 24 h, while the Azna, Goli and Naz lines absorbed the least.
studies.kitchen: Not all dried beans behave the same, even at the same price — one supplier's or lot's kidney beans can drink more water, cook softer, and split more than another's under your exact same soak-and-simmer. Soaking is what buys you shorter cook time and fewer blown-out, mushy beans (splitting = ugly plate plus lost usable yield). If a new bean lot cooks up differently than last month's, that's the variety talking, not your cook — worth tracking which supplier's beans hold together on your line.

studies.authors: Yadav, B. K.; Jindal, V. K.
studies.title: Water uptake and solid loss during cooking of milled rice (Oryza sativa L.) in relation to its physicochemical properties
studies.finding: Cooking 10 Thai milled-rice varieties (16-29% amylose) in excess water, the authors found water uptake climbs quickly at first then flattens as grains approach saturation (uptake curves fit a modified exponential, R2 0.995-0.999), while dissolved solids leach into the cooking water as a power function of cooking time — steadily more the longer it boils. How much water a rice takes up was governed largely by its amylose content and amylose solubility (alkali-spreading score); higher-amylose rices take up more water and need longer cooking.
studies.kitchen: Rice swells because the grain drinks water until it's saturated — that's your cooked yield (dry rice comes back roughly two-and-a-half to three times its weight cooked). But boil it loose in lots of water for too long and starch bleeds out into the pot: you lose yield and get gluey, cloudy water. Match the water to the rice — a firm long-grain (high amylose) wants more water and time than a softer short-grain — and pull it at absorption rather than drown-and-drain if you care about finished weight.

studies.authors: Hu, Z.; Yang, Y.; Lu, L.; Chen, Y.; Zhu, Z.; Huang, J.
studies.title: Kinetics of water absorption expansion of rice during soaking at different temperatures and correlation analysis upon the influential factors
studies.finding: Soaking japonica and indica rice at 25-70 C, the authors tracked how grains take on water and swell over time, fitting five kinetic models to the curves (R2 > 0.97). Both absorption and expansion rise with soak time and temperature until they saturate. Correlation analysis showed apparent amylose content was significantly negatively correlated with the maximum expansion ratio, and protein content was significantly negatively correlated with the water-absorption rate — so a rice's composition sets how much and how fast it swells.
studies.kitchen: Pre-soaking rice front-loads the hydration, so soaked grains cook faster and swell more fully — a lever for consistent portions on a busy line. Warmer soak water hydrates faster than cold. And expect different rices to swell differently: a high-amylose (firm, separate-grain) rice puffs up less than a softer one, and a high-protein rice takes longer to take on water. Switch varieties and your soak time and finished volume shift even at the identical dry weight, so re-check your scoop.

studies.authors: Kader, Adel A.
studies.title: Flavor quality of fruits and vegetables
studies.venue: Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture, 88(11), 1863-1868
studies.finding: A review of what actually makes fruits and vegetables taste good. Eating quality — the balance of sugars, acids, and aroma volatiles — is largely fixed before harvest by the cultivar and by how ripe the item was when it was picked. For most crops, the longer the gap between harvest and eating, the more of that characteristic flavor is lost and the more off-flavors develop. Many commercial crops are harvested less-than-ripe so they survive shipping, which caps how good they can ever taste on the plate.
studies.kitchen: The best-eating window is decided before the crate hits your dock — by variety and by ripeness at picking, not by anything you do in the kitchen. Two levers you actually control: buy each item in its true local season (when it's picked riper and travels less), and shorten the clock from delivery to plate. A tomato or peach that spent a week in transit has already spent its flavor; hold produce cold and turn it fast instead of 'letting it ripen' warm on a shelf, which for most items just ages it rather than sweetening it.

studies.authors: Lee, Seung K.; Kader, Adel A.
studies.title: Preharvest and postharvest factors influencing vitamin C content of horticultural crops
studies.finding: A review of what drives vitamin C (ascorbic acid) levels in produce, before and after harvest. Before harvest: more light/sun during growing raises vitamin C, while heavy nitrogen fertilizer and very high yields tend to lower it, and cultivar and maturity matter. After harvest: vitamin C is fragile — losses accelerate with higher temperature, longer storage time, bruising, and cut surfaces. Prompt cooling and cold storage is the single biggest lever for retaining it.
studies.kitchen: Nutrient density isn't a fixed spec — a head of greens grown in bright season can carry more vitamin C than a dim-winter one, and it bleeds out fast once it's on your shelf. Practical moves: buy for turnover, not stockpiling; get produce into the walk-in the moment it lands (warm time on the back dock is pure vitamin loss); and prep close to service rather than cutting-and-holding, since cut and bruised surfaces lose vitamin C fastest. If a dish is marketed as 'nutritious,' in-season sourcing plus cold-chain plus cut-to-order is what actually backs the claim.

studies.authors: Tieman, Denise M.; Zhu, Guangtao; Resende, Marcio F. R., Jr.; et al. (incl. Klee, Harry J.)
studies.title: A chemical genetic roadmap to improved tomato flavor
studies.finding: Researchers measured flavor chemicals in 398 tomato varieties (modern, heirloom, and wild) and had consumer panels rate them. Modern commercial varieties contain significantly less sugar and significantly lower levels of the key aroma volatiles (and acids) that drive liking than older heirloom types. Decades of breeding for yield, size, firmness, and shelf life inadvertently selected away the chemicals that make a tomato taste like a tomato — a deficiency the authors mapped to specific genetic loci via whole-genome sequencing and a genome-wide association study.
studies.kitchen: The variety on the invoice — not just the season — decides whether a tomato eats flat or vivid. A cheap commodity round is chemically missing the sugars and aromas a flavor-bred or heirloom variety carries, and no amount of salting or roasting fully rebuilds them. When flavor is the whole point (caprese, raw salsa, a tomato salad), spec the cultivar by name and accept the higher cost and shorter shelf life as the price of taste; route the commodity rounds to cooked applications where you're layering flavor anyway. Same lesson across the produce order: ask the supplier for the cultivar, not just 'tomatoes.'

studies.authors: Schwieterman, Michael L.; Colquhoun, Thomas A.; Jaworski, Elizabeth A.; Bartoshuk, Linda M.; Gilbert, Jessica L.; Tieman, Denise M.; Clark, David G.
studies.title: Strawberry flavor: diverse chemical compositions, a seasonal influence, and effects on sensory perception
studies.finding: Across many strawberry varieties and harvest dates, sweetness and overall consumer liking tracked sugar levels and a specific set of aroma volatiles — and both varied substantially with growing season and conditions, with fruit grown under warmer-season pressures generally lower in sucrose and total volatiles. Notably, a subset of volatile compounds made berries taste sweeter than their measured sugar alone would predict. So the very same cultivar can eat noticeably better in a favorable stretch of the season than in a harsh one, independent of price.
studies.kitchen: 'In season' and 'cheapest' are not the same weeks. Berries from the cool front and tail of the local season often eat sweeter and more aromatic than the heat-grown flood-of-supply peak, even at similar or higher cost. Taste before you commit a menu feature — a mid-heatwave flat can be watery and flat even when it's abundant and cheap. Build berry desserts and garnishes around the genuine peak-eating window, and in the off weeks lean on macerating (sugar + acid) or cooking to compensate rather than plating them raw and naked.

studies.authors: Ratkowsky, D.A.; Olley, J.; McMeekin, T.A.; Ball, A.
studies.title: Relationship between temperature and growth rate of bacterial cultures
studies.finding: Bacterial growth rate does not rise in a straight line with temperature. Ratkowsky and colleagues showed that the square root of the growth rate is a straight-line function of temperature above a species-specific notional minimum (T0, usually well below 0 C) — meaning growth rate climbs with roughly the square of how far storage temperature sits above that minimum. The practical upshot: small increases in storage temperature produce disproportionately large increases in how fast bacteria multiply. Near refrigeration temperatures, a rise of only about 5 C (about 9 F) can roughly double the growth rate, though the exact multiple depends on the organism.
studies.kitchen: Shelf life is not a number, it is a number at a temperature. A walk-in holding at 41 F versus 34 F is not a small difference — it can roughly double how fast product spoils, which is why a case that 'should last a week' dies in three or four days when the box runs warm. Stop quoting hold times in the abstract; quote them at the temperature you actually hold. Put a cheap logging thermometer in the walk-in, run it as cold as you safely can (just above freezing), and treat every degree above about 38 F as shelf life you are paying for and throwing away.

studies.authors: Gram, L.; Ravn, L.; Rasch, M.; Bruhn, J.B.; Christensen, A.B.; Givskov, M.
studies.title: Food spoilage—interactions between food spoilage bacteria
studies.finding: However varied the raw material, the microbes that actually spoil a food are a small, predictable subset — the 'specific spoilage organisms' — and which ones win is set by a few storage parameters: temperature, packaging atmosphere, water activity, and pH. These dominant spoilers, not the total microbial count, produce the off-odors and slime that mark the end of shelf life, and they interact (including via cell-to-cell chemical signaling) as the population builds. Because the same conditions breed the same spoilers, the spoilage flora that develops during storage can be predicted from how the food is stored.
studies.kitchen: Spoilage is not random luck — the same storage conditions breed the same spoilers every time, so you control shelf life by controlling the box, not by hoping. Colder holding, tighter or modified-atmosphere packaging, and drier surfaces (pat proteins dry, don't let product sit in standing liquid) all tilt the odds toward the slow spoilers. It also means the smell test is legitimate science: the off-odor is the specific spoilage organism hitting its threshold. When it's there, the product is done — regardless of the date printed on the case.

studies.authors: Junttila, J.R.; Niemelä, S.I.; Hirn, J.
studies.title: Minimum growth temperatures of Listeria monocytogenes and non-haemolytic listeria
studies.finding: Testing 78 strains of the foodborne pathogen Listeria monocytogenes plus non-pathogenic listeria in a temperature-gradient incubator, the authors found L. monocytogenes kept growing at temperatures down to a mean minimum of about +1.7 C (roughly 35 F) — well within the range of an ordinary refrigerator, and about 0.6 C lower than the non-pathogenic strains. Refrigeration therefore slows this pathogen but does not stop it: given enough time in the cold, it still multiplies.
studies.kitchen: A cold walk-in is not a safe harbor. Dangerous bacteria like Listeria keep growing at normal fridge temperatures — just slowly — so 'it stayed cold the whole time' is not the same as 'it's safe.' This is exactly why ready-to-eat, no-further-cook items (deli meats, smoked fish, cut melon, soft cheeses, prepped salads) get hard date limits and get tossed on schedule even when they still look and smell fine. For those items, time in the cold is a countdown, not a pause — spoilage-clean does not mean safe.

studies.authors: Nychas, G.-J.E.; Skandamis, P.N.; Tassou, C.C.; Koutsoumanis, K.P.
studies.title: Meat spoilage during distribution
studies.finding: This widely cited review of fresh-meat spoilage across the supply chain identifies temperature as the single most important factor governing how fast meat spoils. Spoilage is driven by a specific group of bacteria (the ephemeral or specific spoilage organisms) whose growth — and the off-odors, discoloration, and slime they cause — is largely controlled by storage temperature, oxygen and packaging, and the initial contamination load. Hold it colder and spoilage is slower; break the cold chain, even briefly, and that growth is not recovered.
studies.kitchen: For proteins, the cold chain IS the shelf life. Meat left on a warm loading dock, or a walk-in that drifts up overnight, is quietly spending days of usable life you already paid for on the invoice. Receive cold (check case temperature at the door and reject warm deliveries), get product into the coldest holding fast, rotate FIFO, and don't judge freshness by the sell-by date alone — judge it by how the cold chain was actually held. A tight cold chain is far cheaper than the spoiled cases it prevents.
